front.title: Scoping the AUDIT Use Case for Transparent Measurement Evidence of AI Systems

abstract.t: This document scopes a use case for the SCITT architecture: the AUDIT use case, in which measurements of AI systems are published as transparent, append-only, verifiable evidence. It defines a state vocabulary for the lifecycle of a piece of measurement evidence, from DISCOVERED through SETTLED, with UNCHECKABLE as an honest terminal state for evidence whose verification chain is broken or absent. The document distinguishes measurement from certification throughout: the evidence described here records what was measured, by whom, with which key, anchored where, and says nothing about whether the measured system is good. This document specifies nothing and proposes no wire format. It scopes a use case and defines vocabulary, and identifies the existing protocol machinery that already carries each state.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: The SCITT architecture describes how signed statements about artifacts are made transparent: statements are registered in an append-only ledger and receipts are issued that bind a statement to a position in that ledger. The architecture is neutral about what the statements are about.

A growing class of systems—AI models, agent frameworks, and the services built on them—are subjects of measurement: someone runs a benchmark, an evaluation, a census, or a probe, and records a result. Today those results travel as claims. A claim's weight is a function of the recipient's trust in the claimant, which is not a verifiable property. The AUDIT use case is the application of SCITT transparency to that class: measurement results are issued as signed statements, registered, witnessed, and anchored, so that what is trusted is a signature, a ledger position, and an anchor—not the say-so of the measuring party.

The motivation is not regulatory. Several jurisdictions are constructing obligations that will produce demand for durable, checkable records of what was measured about which system and when (for example, the EU AI Act's record-keeping provisions and the NIST AI RMF's measurement function). This document does not map to any such obligation. It scopes the use case on its own terms.

The document does three things: it bounds the use case (), it defines a state vocabulary for evidence lifecycle (), and it identifies which existing machinery carries each state (). It specifies nothing.

section.title: Conventions and Definitions
section.t: This document is Informational and contains no normative requirements.

dd.t: The execution of a defined procedure against a defined subject, producing a recorded result. Measurement is distinguished from certification, which is a judgement about fitness for purpose. This document concerns measurement only.
A structured document recording one measurement: subject, procedure, inputs, result, timestamp, and the identity of the measuring party. A card is the unit of signing.
A measurement card together with the cryptographic artifacts that make it checkable: signature, ledger receipt, witness records, and anchors.
A Merkle root computed over an ordered set of leaf digests, each leaf being the digest of one measurement card. The root is the unit of anchoring.

A third party that countersigns or includes a digest in an independent, publicly auditable log, such that the digest's existence at a point in time can be checked without reference to the measuring party.
A timestamping commitment to a digest on a widely replicated substrate whose history is impractical to rewrite, such as a public blockchain via OpenTimestamps .

section.title: The AUDIT Use Case
section.t: The use case has four actors:

ul.li: The measuring party, who runs procedures and issues cards.
The subject provider, whose system is measured and who may or may not cooperate.
The transparency service, operating an append-only ledger per , which registers signed statements and issues receipts.
The verifier, who later checks the evidence. The verifier is assumed to be offline-capable and unwilling to create an account with anyone.

section.t: The use case's distinguishing properties, relative to the supply-chain cases SCITT was designed around, are:

ul.li: The subject is not a software artifact with a stable digest. An AI model served behind an API may change without notice. Evidence must therefore record what was actually observed, with the observation timestamp, and must tolerate the subject having changed since. A card about a model is a claim about an observation session, not about a persistent object.

The measurement may be adversarially unwelcome. The subject provider may prefer that a measurement not exist. This places the burden on durability: a card that exists only on the measuring party's web server can be made to disappear by anyone with leverage over that server. Registration in an independent ledger, third-party witnessing, and anchoring each reduce the set of parties who can silently erase the record.

The value of the evidence is in its checkability, not its conclusion. Two honest measuring parties running the same procedure should get compatible results, and the AUDIT use case wants a state (REPRODUCED, ) that records when that has happened—and an honest state (UNCHECKABLE, ) for when the chain needed to check the evidence does not exist.

section.t: The use case explicitly excludes: grading, ranking, certification, conformity assessment, and any statement of fitness for purpose. Those may be built on top of measurement evidence by other parties; they are not part of the evidence.

section.title: A State Vocabulary for Measurement Evidence
section.t: The states below describe where a piece of evidence is in its lifecycle. They are descriptive, not normative: a state is a fact about what has been done, checkable from the artifacts, and carries no quality judgement. The vocabulary exists so that a measuring party can report its posture honestly and a verifier can see at a glance which properties hold.

The states form a partial order for the forward path, but the vocabulary's usefulness is precisely that states can be absent: a card may be SIGNED but never ROOTED, and saying so is more informative than saying nothing.

section.title: Discovery and Indexing States

dd.t: A subject of potential measurement interest has been identified. No procedure has run. No evidence exists. This state exists so that census-style work— enumerating a population before measuring it—can be reported without implying that measurement has occurred.

The subject has been assigned a stable local identifier and its discovery metadata (where found, when, under what description) has been recorded. Still no measurement. The distinction from DISCOVERED is bookkeeping: the subject is now addressable in later cards.

A defined procedure has executed against the subject and produced a recorded result. The result exists as a measurement card but is unsigned. A MEASURED card is a draft: it has no integrity protection and no bound identity, and should be treated by any consumer as unverifiable.

section.t: The forward transition from MEASURED that never happens is common and legitimate: much exploratory measurement is not worth the cost of signing. The vocabulary does not require every card to advance.

section.title: Signing and Aggregation States

dd.t: The card has been signed by the measuring party with a key whose verification method is resolvable (for example, an Ed25519 key published at a DID, or a COSE key in a discoverable location). The signature binds the card's bytes to the signer. It is an integrity claim, not a truth claim: it says these bytes are the bytes that were signed, and says nothing about whether the measurement inside them is correct.

The card's digest has been included as a leaf in a Merkle tree whose root has been published, together with the inclusion path. Aggregation is the scaling mechanism: one root commits to many cards, so the cost of later witnessing and anchoring is paid once per root, not once per card. A verifier who holds the root, the leaf index, and the path can check inclusion without trusting the publisher, provided the root itself is checkable. ROOTED therefore inherits the checkability of whatever state the root has reached.

section.t: A card may be SIGNED without being ROOTED (a one-off measurement published alone) and a root may be published without the card being individually SIGNED (the signature may live at the root). The vocabulary deliberately does not force a single pipeline shape.

section.title: Witnessing and Anchoring States

dd.t: The card's digest (or the root containing it) has been submitted to a public transparency log—in the running implementation, Rekor —and an inclusion proof has been obtained. The witness is a third party with an independent, auditable, append-only log. After this state, the evidence's existence at the witnessed time no longer depends on the measuring party's infrastructure surviving.

An OpenTimestamps commitment to the root has been created and submitted for inclusion in a Bitcoin transaction, but the transaction is not yet confirmed. The calendar portion of the proof exists; the blockchain portion is pending. This state is named explicitly because an unconfirmed timestamp is weaker than a confirmed one, and conflating the two is a known way to overstate evidence strength.

The OpenTimestamps commitment is confirmed on the Bitcoin chain to a depth the verifier considers adequate. The timestamp is now backed by the cost of rewriting Bitcoin history, which is the strongest widely available not-belonging-to-anyone clock.

section.t: The two states are separate so that a pipeline can report "timestamp submitted, awaiting confirmation" without borrowing the credibility of a confirmation it does not yet have.

dd.t: The evidence chain is complete for this card: SIGNED, ROOTED, WITNESSED_REKOR, and CONFIRMED_BITCOIN all hold, and the published artifacts are sufficient for an offline verifier to check every link without contacting the measuring party. SETTLED is a statement about the evidence, not about the measured subject.

An independent party, using the published procedure and inputs, has repeated the measurement and obtained a result within the published tolerance, and that reproduction is itself signed and published. REPRODUCED is the only state that says anything about the measurement's content: it says two parties agree on what the procedure yields. It still says nothing about fitness.

A terminal state assigned honestly when the chain required to check the evidence does not exist: a lost key, a dead witness log, a root whose leaves are no longer published, a card whose signer cannot be resolved. UNCHECKABLE is not an accusation; it is a refusal to borrow credibility. An evidence corpus that reports UNCHECKABLE where it applies is more trustworthy than one whose every entry is labelled checkable, because the label then means something.

section.title: Evidence Artifacts
section.t: The use case's running implementation publishes, for each card:

ul.li: the measurement card itself, as a structured JSON document addressed by content digest;
an Ed25519 signature over the card bytes, with the verification key published at a resolvable location;
a published chain of signed checkpoints over the card index, so that the index itself is tamper-evident;
a Merkle root per publication batch, with inclusion paths;
Rekor inclusion proofs for roots;
OpenTimestamps proofs for roots, with pending and confirmed states distinguished as in .

section.t: The artifacts are listed here to make the vocabulary concrete, not to standardize their formats. COSE_Sign1 is the obvious carrier for signed cards in a SCITT context; the implementation above predates that choice and uses raw Ed25519 over JSON. Both are instances of the same state machine. Where a digest over wire octets is used as an identifier, the framing considerations of apply.

section.title: What Transparency Buys Here
section.t: Transparency infrastructure earns its cost in this use case in four specific ways:

ul.li: Non-erasure. A card registered in an independent ledger and witnessed in an independent log cannot be quietly withdrawn by the measuring party, and cannot be made to disappear by pressure on the measuring party alone. For measurements that are adversarially unwelcome (), this is the primary property.

Back-dating resistance. A measurement anchored before an event (a model release, an incident, a regulatory deadline) can be shown to predate it. A measurement claimed after the fact to have been made before the fact cannot be retro-fitted, because the anchor is missing. This is what converts "we measured this" from a claim into a checkable fact about timing.

Selective-disclosure detection. A measuring party that publishes roots but shows only favourable cards can be caught: the root commits to a leaf count, and a verifier with the full leaf set can check what was omitted. The vocabulary's INDEXED state, reported honestly, makes the denominator visible.

Verifier independence. A SETTLED card can be checked by a party with no relationship to the measurer, no account, and no network access to the measurer. The verifier's trust is placed in signature verification, the witness log's append-only property, and the anchoring chain's replication—all of which are independently auditable.

section.t: What transparency does not buy is correctness. A wrong measurement, transparently published, is a wrong measurement that cannot be erased. That is the point: the infrastructure makes the record durable and checkable, and the measuring party's incentive to be right comes from exactly that durability.

section.title: Relationship to Existing Work
section.t: Each state in is carried by machinery that already exists:

ul.li: SIGNED maps to a SCITT signed statement per , Section 5, with COSE_Sign1 as the carrier.
Registration and receipts map to the SCITT Reference APIs and to COSE receipt profiles such as .

WITNESSED_REKOR uses the Sigstore Rekor public instance , which is not SCITT infrastructure but is an independent append-only log with public inclusion proofs; the vocabulary cares about the property, not the operator.
STAMPED_PENDING_BITCOIN and CONFIRMED_BITCOIN use OpenTimestamps , which aggregates many digests into one chain transaction, making per-card anchoring economically feasible.
The framing hazards for digest-based identifiers over CBOR objects are measured in the sibling document , which this document cites rather than repeats.

section.t: This document discovers nothing in that machinery. It names the states so that an evidence corpus can describe its own posture in terms a verifier can act on, and so that gaps (a SIGNED card that is never ROOTED, a stamp that never confirms) are reportable rather than silent.

section.title: Honesty and Scope
section.t: This section states what this document does not claim.

ul.li: This document does not define a certification scheme. No state in is a judgement that a measured system is adequate, safe, lawful, or fit for any purpose. The vocabulary describes evidence handling, not merit.

This document does not claim the vocabulary is complete. Other witnesses (other transparency logs, other anchoring chains) map onto the same shape; the names given here are the ones the running implementation uses.
This document does not claim that any state has been achieved for any particular corpus by any particular party. It defines labels; it does not assert facts.
This document does not propose protocol changes to SCITT, Sigstore, or OpenTimestamps. It uses them as they are.

The author operates a measurement service that uses this vocabulary. The document is offered as a scope and a set of definitions, not as evidence of the service's quality, and no conclusion about the service follows from anything written here.

section.title: Security Considerations
section.t: The security properties of the states are inherited from their carriers: Ed25519 signatures, Merkle inclusion, Rekor's append-only log, and Bitcoin's replication. None are weakened by the vocabulary.

Two hazards are worth stating. First, a vocabulary of honest states can be used dishonestly: a party may label a card SETTLED when it is not. The defence is structural—every state is checkable from published artifacts, so the label is a claim, and the check is cheap. Second, the UNCHECKABLE state can be abused in reverse, to disparage a competitor's evidence; the check for that is the same, since UNCHECKABLE is also a claim about artifacts and can be verified or refuted by inspection.

section.name: Acknowledgements
section.t: The state vocabulary was developed against a running evidence pipeline, which is the surest way to discover which states need honest names. The SCITT working group's published architecture and reference APIs carry every forward state defined here.
